items.prompt: How confident are you that you could describe a screen as information, actions, state and feedback rather than just how it looks?
Why is a beautiful screen connected to nothing called a demo rather than a product?

options.label: Because the frontend is the control surface for the rest of the system; without real actions, state and feedback behind it, nothing is being operated
Because it was built too quickly

items.explanation: The frontend is the surface through which a person operates the application; if no system sits behind the controls, the screen is only demonstrating an idea.

items.prompt: Pick one screen you use often, such as a chat, a lobby or a search page. Label four things on it as information, action, state or feedback, one of each.

criteria: Names one concrete example of each of the four parts
Puts remembered things such as open tabs or typed text under state, not information

items.prompt: In your own words, explain why frontend architecture is more than decoration.

criteria: Explains that the frontend controls what the user can see, do and understand about the system
Notes that weak design makes a working system unusable

items.prompt: How confident are you that you could list the states an important screen needs, beyond the successful one?
A heart icon turns red the instant it is tapped, before any server answer. What is this called, and what must the app be ready to do?

options.label: A confirmed save; nothing else is needed
An optimistic update; the app must undo it or show an error if the request fails
An offline state; the app must block the tap

items.explanation: Optimistic updates show success early for speed, and the design must include undoing the change or reporting the failure when the server disagrees.

items.prompt: Choose one important screen, such as a search page or a submission form. List the states it needs and write one line describing what the user sees in each. Cover at least initial, loading, success, empty and error.

criteria: Names at least five distinct states
Describes what the user sees or can do in each state

items.prompt: In your own words, explain why a visible change on the screen is not proof that an action succeeded.

criteria: Explains that the frontend can render a change before the server confirms it
Mentions the app must handle failure afterwards, such as undoing an optimistic update

items.prompt: How confident are you that you could choose whether frontend information should be screen state, browser-saved, URL state or server-saved?
A student wants to send a friend a link to an events page with city and category filters already applied. Which level of memory makes that possible?

options.label: Screen state held inside the open page
URL state, with the filters stored in the shareable address
An unsaved form on the student's device

items.explanation: Filters stored in the URL are rebuilt when anyone opens the link, so the exact view can be bookmarked and shared.

items.prompt: Take a form or feature where users enter real work. Write down every way the user could lose that work, then choose for each whether it needs submit-only saving, a draft button, auto-save or just a warning.

criteria: Identifies at least two ways work could be lost, such as refresh or device switch
Assigns a protection that matches each risk
Explains the choice rather than defaulting to auto-save for everything

items.prompt: In your own words, explain the difference between temporary screen state and server-saved information, with one example of each.

criteria: Explains that screen state dies with the page while server-saved data follows the account
Gives a correct example of each, such as unsaved form text versus a submitted registration

items.prompt: How confident are you that you could complete the button test for every clickable element on a screen you design?
Which is the stronger instruction to a coding agent?

options.label: Build me a modern page for finding local activities.
Propose three layouts for the discovery page, compare their tradeoffs, recommend the simplest option, list the reusable components, and describe every state before writing code.
Add a form and a Submit button.

items.explanation: The strong instruction makes the agent compare options and define states before building; the weak ones make it invent the product.

items.prompt: Pick one button in an app you use. Complete the sentence: 'When the user presses this button, the frontend should ___, the backend should ___, and the user should see ___.'

criteria: Names a frontend reaction, a backend job and a user-visible result
Includes what the user sees if the action fails

items.prompt: In your own words, explain why asking an agent to compare three interface options beats asking it to build the first one immediately.

criteria: Explains that different layouts have different tradeoffs tied to the user's decision
Notes that comparing first prevents premature code and surfaces a simpler MVP
